planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Blackbeard is a Walters Gardens selection of foxglove beardtongue grown chiefly for its near-black, deep purple-bronze foliage, one of the darkest of any Penstemon digitalis cultivar.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; foliage color darkens most fully with several hours of direct sun. Blackbeard produces glossy, near-black purple-bronze leaves on unusually tall, sturdy stems that hold pale lavender-pink, tubular flowers well above the foliage clump in early summer, giving it more height and drama than the shorter, more widely planted Husker Red. Hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees work the flowers readily, and the dark foliage remains an asset in the border long after bloom finishes. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the plant and avoid rich, wet soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Springs is a compact, vegetatively propagated selection of foothill penstemon chosen for its especially intense, saturated blue flower color.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Blue Springs needs the same excellent drainage as the species and struggles in heavy or overwatered soil. This selection keeps the electric blue-violet flower color of the best wild foothill penstemon populations while staying noticeably shorter and more compact than seed-grown plants, making it better suited to small beds, containers, and the front of a border. Bees and hummingbirds visit the tubular flowers heavily from late spring into summer. Shear lightly after the first flush to tidy the mound and encourage a second round of bloom, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which shortens the plant's life.

common_name: Pygmy Hairy Beardtongue (Dwarf Rock Garden Penstemon)

planting.note: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Pygmaeus is a long-stable dwarf strain of hairy beardtongue only a few inches tall, ideal for rock gardens and edging.

directions: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; this dwarf strain comes reasonably true from seed and is widely grown from the trade as a true rock-garden miniature of hairy beardtongue. Compact tufts of hairy, toothed foliage send up short spikes of pale lavender-violet, tubular flowers with a fuzzy white palate in late spring, at a fraction of the height of the straight species. Its diminutive scale suits it to trough gardens, rock garden crevices, and the front edge of a dry border where full-size penstemons would overwhelm the setting. Avoid rich, moist soil or heavy mulch, both of which encourage rot and rank, floppy growth out of character for this naturally tight, tidy selection.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Novastar Red is a compact, uniform seed strain of Penstemon barbatus bred to flower reliably in its first year from an early sowing.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since penstemon is prone to crown rot in wet, heavy soil. Novastar Red bears dense, upright spikes of saturated scarlet-red, tubular flowers on a compact, uniform plant bred from seed for a tidy, garden-ready habit shorter than older open-pollinated Penstemon barbatus strains. Hummingbirds visit the hot-colored flowers throughout the long summer bloom season, and the plant tolerates heat and drought well once established. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong flowering, and avoid rich soil or heavy fertilizer, which produces weak, floppy growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Coccineus is a long-cultivated, taller selection of Penstemon barbatus with true scarlet-red flowers, an RHS Award of Garden Merit holder.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since penstemon is prone to crown rot in wet, heavy soil. Coccineus is an old, garden-worthy selection of Penstemon barbatus valued for pure scarlet-red, tubular flowers held on tall, willowy spikes well above narrow gray-green foliage, taller and more airy in habit than modern dwarf bedding strains. It is a superb hummingbird plant through its long early-to-midsummer bloom season and holds up well in a mixed perennial border without staking. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage rebloom, and avoid heavy, wet soil or excess fertilizer, both of which shorten the plant's life.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Garnet (sold as 'Andenken an Friedrich Hahn') is a classic hybrid border penstemon with deep wine-red flowers and an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in full sun; Garnet tolerates slightly richer, moister soil than most western native penstemons but still needs good drainage to avoid winter crown rot. This long-popular hybrid bears wiry, branching spikes of deep, glowing wine-red, tubular flowers from midsummer well into fall, one of the longest bloom seasons of any hardy border penstemon, and draws bees and hummingbirds throughout. In colder parts of its range it benefits from a dry winter mulch of grit or evergreen boughs, and cutting the old growth back hard in early spring rather than fall improves winter survival. Deadhead through summer to keep new flower spikes coming.
scientific_name_note: Widely sold under the trade name 'Garnet'; the correct cultivar name is 'Andenken an Friedrich Hahn'.

common_name: Sour Grapes Penstemon (Smoky Blue-Purple Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sour Grapes is a hardy hybrid penstemon noted for its unusual, iridescent grayish blue-purple flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; good drainage protects the crown through wet winters, a common failure point for hybrid border penstemons. Sour Grapes bears loose spikes of smoky, slate-blue to dusty purple flowers with a faint iridescent sheen, an unusual muted color that reads almost gray-lavender from a distance and stands apart from the hot pinks and reds typical of the genus. Bees work the tubular flowers steadily from midsummer into fall, and the plant combines well with silver-foliage companions that echo its cool coloring. Cut back hard in spring rather than fall, and avoid heavy or waterlogged soil, which the crown does not tolerate through winter.

common_name: Windwalker Pink Penstemon (Silver-Foliaged Long-Blooming Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Windwalker Pink, a Plant Select introduction, is a Great Plains native hybrid bred for an unusually long summer bloom season and silvery, drought-tolerant foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, since penstemon is prone to crown rot in wet, heavy soil. Windwalker Pink bears tall, branching spikes of clear pink, tubular flowers over soft, silvery-gray foliage, blooming continuously from early summer well into fall — a much longer display than most hardy penstemon hybrids offer. Bred from Great Plains native species, it is exceptionally heat and drought tolerant once established and thrives on minimal supplemental water. Deadhead spent spikes periodically to keep new flowers coming, and avoid rich soil or excess fertilizer, which produces weak, floppy growth.
sources: Plant Select — Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cascade penstemon is one of the few penstemons that tolerates woodland-edge shade and regular summer moisture without decline.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most dryland penstemons, this Pacific Northwest native tolerates regular moisture and open woodland shade without crown rot. Toothed, glossy green leaves form low clumps topped in early to midsummer by dense, whorled clusters of deep violet-blue, tubular flowers that draw bumblebees and hummingbirds along forest edges, subalpine meadows, and roadside clearings from the Cascades to the coast. Its tolerance for cool, moist, partly shaded sites makes it a useful choice for a woodland garden border or native plant bed where full-sun penstemons would struggle. Water during dry summer spells and avoid heavy clay that stays saturated through winter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; broadleaf penstemon is one of the more shade-tolerant western species, native to open woods and forest clearings rather than dry rock outcrops.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; broadleaf penstemon grows naturally in open Pacific Northwest woodlands and forest clearings and tolerates more shade and moisture than most western penstemons. It is easily distinguished from other native penstemons by its broad, toothed, egg-shaped leaves, quite unlike the narrow linear foliage typical of the genus, and sends up branching stems of bright violet-blue flowers with a white-haired throat in late spring to early summer. Its woodland-edge origin makes it a good choice for a partly shaded native plant border or the sunnier fringe of a woodland garden, sites where full-sun dryland penstemons perform poorly. Provide summer moisture during establishment and avoid deep, permanent shade, which reduces flowering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; littleflower penstemon is a low, mat-forming alpine and subalpine species from high meadows and rocky slopes across the western mountains.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun; this small alpine species needs the same fast drainage it gets in its native rocky meadows and talus slopes. Slender stems form low, spreading mats topped in early summer by tight, whorled clusters of small, deep blue-violet to purple flowers, disproportionately abundant for the plant's diminutive scale, native to high mountain meadows and rocky ridges from the Rockies to the Cascades and Sierra Nevada. Its cushion-forming habit and cold hardiness make it an excellent choice for a trough garden, rock garden crevice, or alpine scree bed. Avoid rich or poorly drained soil, both of which cause rapid decline in this lean-soil, high-elevation specialist.
